title: Binary search
starter: Think of a number between 1 and 100. How many yes/no questions would a friend need to guess it? What is the best question to ask first?
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: How it works
facts: Check the middle item of the list.
If it matches, stop. If the target is larger, discard the lower half; if smaller, discard the upper half.
Repeat on what is left until you find it or nothing remains.
stations.challenge: Describe a binary search in four steps of your own.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Check the middle item of the list.
Also credit: If it matches, stop. If the target is larger, discard the lower half; if smaller, discard the upper half.

questions.q: Step through a binary search for 23. Tap each item the algorithm checks, in order.
Which item does a binary search look at first?

stations.name: The one condition
facts: The list must be in order, or the algorithm cannot know which half to discard.
If the data is unsorted, it must be sorted first, which takes time.
Sorting once and searching many times is the situation where it pays.
stations.challenge: Explain why a binary search cannot be used on an unsorted list.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: The list must be in order, or the algorithm cannot know which half to discard.
Also credit: If the data is unsorted, it must be sorted first, which takes time.

questions.q: Why must the list be sorted?
questions.a: Comparing with the middle only tells you which half to keep if the order is known

questions.q: When is sorting first, then binary searching, worth the effort?
questions.a: When the same list will be searched many times

stations.name: Why it is so fast
facts: Each comparison halves what is left.
A list of 1,000 items takes about 10 checks; a million takes about 20.
Doubling the list adds one comparison, not a thousand.
stations.challenge: Work out roughly how many checks a binary search needs for 64 items.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Each comparison halves what is left.
Also credit: A list of 1,000 items takes about 10 checks; a million takes about 20.

questions.q: A sorted list has 1,000,000 items. Roughly how many checks does a binary search need?
A list doubles in size. What happens to a binary search?

stations.name: Comparing the two searches
facts: Linear: any order, simple, slow on large data.
Binary: must be sorted, more complex, very fast on large data.
For a handful of items the difference doesn't matter; for millions it decides whether the system works.
stations.challenge: Make a table comparing linear and binary search on three points.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Linear: any order, simple, slow on large data.
Also credit: Binary: must be sorted, more complex, very fast on large data.

questions.q: Does each statement describe a linear search or a binary search?
questions.a: Works on a list in any order = Linear search; Requires a sorted list = Binary search; Checks each item in turn = Linear search; Halves the list each time = Binary search; About 20 checks for a million items = Binary search; Up to a million checks for a million items = Linear search

questions.q: Which search would you use on 30 items that are constantly reordered?
questions.a: Linear, because keeping them sorted would cost more than it saves

stations.name: Writing it down
facts: Keep two pointers: left at 0 and right at the last index.
The midpoint is (left + right) divided by two, rounded down.
Move left or right past the midpoint depending on the comparison.
stations.challenge: Write pseudocode for a binary search.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Keep two pointers: left at 0 and right at the last index.
Also credit: The midpoint is (left + right) divided by two, rounded down.

questions.q: Put these lines into a working binary search.
questions.a: left = 0 and right = the last index → while left is less than or equal to right →   mid = (left + right) DIV 2 →   if list[mid] is the target then stop, found →   if the target is larger, set left = mid + 1 →   otherwise set right = mid - 1 → endwhile

questions.q: Why is DIV, or integer division, used for the midpoint?
questions.a: An index must be a whole number

stations.name: Answering binary search questions
facts: Always state that the list must be sorted: it is usually worth a mark.
Describe the midpoint comparison and the discarding of half.
If asked to show the steps, write down the midpoint checked at each stage.
stations.challenge: Plan a five-mark answer describing a binary search on a list of 15 names.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Always state that the list must be sorted: it is usually worth a mark.
Also credit: Describe the midpoint comparison and the discarding of half.

questions.q: Find 66 with a binary search. Tap each item the algorithm checks.
Which is the strongest description of a binary search?
questions.a: On a sorted list, it compares the middle item with the target and discards the half that cannot contain it, repeating until found

final.name: Final challenge: halve it

questions.q: Which search suits each situation better?
questions.a: Fifteen names in no order = Linear search; A sorted phone directory of a million entries = Binary search; A list rebuilt from scratch every second = Linear search; A sorted index searched constantly = Binary search; Searching unsorted data once = Linear search; A sorted list of ten thousand product codes = Binary search

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Describe how a binary search works.
points: For a handful of items the difference doesn't matter; for millions it decides whether the system works.
Describe the midpoint comparison and the discarding of half.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 4.

exam.q: State the condition a list must meet before a binary search can be used.
points: Always state that the list must be sorted: it is usually worth a mark.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark for a correct answer.

exam.q: A sorted list contains 1,000 items. Compare the number of comparisons needed by a linear search and a binary search in the worst case.
points: A list of 1,000 items takes about 10 checks; a million takes about 20.
If the data is unsorted, it must be sorted first, which takes time.
Binary: must be sorted, more complex, very fast on large data.
For a handful of items the difference doesn't matter; for millions it decides whether the system works.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 4.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
